reaction_equations: DEZn pulse ¼ surface /C0 OH þ C2H5 /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 ! surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 þ C2H6
Water pulse ¼ surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 þ H2O ! surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 OH þ C2H6
surface_mechanism_description: Hydrogen introduced by the water precursor, in the form of –OH groups, is relatively weakly bounded in the ZnO film and can be removed by a 3 min annealing at 800 /C14 C in oxygen atmosphere. On the other hand, hydrogen introduced by the diethylzinc precursor, in the form of –C2H5 chemical groups, is much more stable and a significant part of it remains in the ZnO films even after RTP annealing at 800 /C14 C.
evidence: The ALD cycle used in the present study consists of two chemical reactions. DEZn pulse ¼ surface /C0 OH þ C2H5 /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 ! surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 þ C2H6 (1) Water pulse ¼ surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 C2H5 þ H2O ! surface /C0 O /C0 Zn /C0 OH þ C2H6 (2) Both precursors used contain hydrogen and this, as already stated, can lead to unintentional incorporation of hydrogen into films during growth. Indeed, as mentioned in the introduction, a high hydrogen content is typically reported for ZnO films grown by ALD. In detail, the reported hydrogen concentration varies from /C25 1020 to /C25 1021 at cm/C0 3 in as-grown ZnO films and can be reduced to /C25 1019 at cm/C0 3 after 3 min of annealing at 800 /C14 C. SIMS profiles measured in the present study reveal that the average hydrogen content in the as-grown ZnO samples of the H series varies bewteen /C25 2.5 /C2 1020 and /C25 1.1 /C2 1021 at cm/C0 3 (with the hydrogen profile in the H100 sample shown in Figure 2 a) and decreases with increasing growth temperature, as previously reported. The same trend is observed in the D series for both hydrogen and deuterium, thus indicating that hydrogen residuals originating from both the unreacted metalorganic ligands and –OH groups actually decrease with increasing Tg. Furthermore, in this case, the hydrogen concentration is found to be lower, between /C25 5.7 /C2 1019 and /C25 3.5 /C2 1020 at cm/C0 3, in agreement with DEZn being the only source of hydrogen contamination into the films (see also Figure 2b). The amount of deuterium in the latter samples varies between /C25 1.1 /C2 1020 and /C25 4.1 /C2 1020 at cm/C0 3 (see Table 1). In fact, deuterium traces that are naturally present in water are also found in the H series with a hydrogen-to-deuterium concentration ratio equal to /C25 1.1–1.2 /C2 104. Finally, here it is worth pointing out that the cumulative hydrogen plus deuterium content in the D series is a factor /C25 0.6–0.7 lower than that in the H series. On the basis of the present results it is not possible to determine the exact origin of the reduced incorporation of hydrogen and/or deuterium in the D series as compared with the H series, even though, also in this case, the kinetic isotope effect might play a role.
